Definitions used in this course (always correct; never change or restate them differently): turnaround time = completion time − arrival time; waiting time = turnaround time − burst time (= completion − arrival − burst); response time = time of first start on the CPU − arrival time; a LOWER priority number means a HIGHER priority; ties are broken by arrival time, then process number; FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive priority never interrupt a running process, while SRTF, preemptive priority and Round Robin can.

Context from the course material:
[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[3] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) [SJF])
burst counts. Preemptive SJF is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). When a new process arrives with a next CPU burst shorter than what is left of the currently executing process, SRTF preempts the running process. Non-preemptive SJF lets the running process finish its burst. P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with burst 4, P3 at 2 with burst 9, P4 at 3 with burst 5. P1 starts at 0. At time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted. Starvation under SJF. A long process can wait indefinitely if short processes keep arriving, because there is always a shorter job to pick; this is starvation (indefinite blocking). SRTF makes it worse because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly.

Context from the course material:
[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise preemptive Priority in a few lines. [Priority])
Priority scheduling (preemptive) always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). It is preemptive: a newly arrived process with a strictly higher priority takes the CPU immediately. On starvation, it can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Its average waiting time is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, and its context-switch overhead is higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise non-preemptive Priority in a few lines. [Priority])
Priority scheduling (non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: a higher-priority arrival waits until the running process finishes. On starvation, it can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Its average waiting time is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do I order the queue in Round Robin when a process arrives at the same time as a quantum expires? [Round Robin])
The newly arrived process goes into the ready queue before the preempted process is placed at the back. So if P3 arrives at exactly the moment P1's quantum ends, the queue becomes P3 followed by P1. This rule is a common source of mistakes in Round Robin numericals.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise Round Robin in a few lines. [Round Robin])
Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Its average waiting time is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn, and its context-switch overhead is the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says in Round Robin the preempted process goes back to the queue before a process that arrives at the same moment. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No. When a process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the new arrival is added to the ready queue first and the preempted process is placed behind it. Putting them in the wrong order is the most common error in Round Robin numericals, and it changes every waiting time after that point.

Context from the course material:
[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the degree of multiprogramming? [Comparison])
The degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes held in memory at once, ready to compete for the CPU. The long-term scheduler controls it by deciding how many new jobs are admitted. Too low a degree leaves the CPU idle between bursts because there are not enough ready processes to switch to; too high a degree can exhaust memory or make each process wait too long for its turn. CPU scheduling algorithms such as FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin operate on whichever processes the long-term scheduler has already admitted.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between the long-term, medium-term and short-term scheduler? [Comparison])
The long-term (job) scheduler decides which jobs are admitted into memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming. The short-term (CPU) scheduler decides which ready process runs on the CPU next and runs very frequently, so it must be fast. The medium-term scheduler swaps processes out of memory and back in to reduce the degree of multiprogramming. The algorithms FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are all short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the types of schedulers? [Comparison])
There are three types of schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler, which admits jobs into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming; the medium-term scheduler, which swaps processes out of and back into memory; and the short-term (CPU) scheduler, which chooses the next ready process to run and runs very often. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the effect of Round Robin on average waiting time? [Round Robin])
The average waiting time under Round Robin is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn.

Since the scheduler cannot know the future, it predicts the next burst as an exponential average of the past ones: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). Here t(n) is the actual length of the most recent burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α is between 0 and 1, commonly 1/2. SJF associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst and gives the CPU to the process with the smallest next burst. If two processes have the same burst length, FCFS order breaks the tie. With α = 0 recent history has no effect; with α = 1 only the last burst counts. Preemptive SJF is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for response time? [General])
Response time = time of the first start on the CPU − arrival time. It measures how long a process waits before it first gets the CPU. In non-preemptive algorithms it equals the waiting time.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for the response ratio in HRRN? [General])
Response ratio = (waiting time + burst time) / burst time. HRRN runs the ready process with the highest response ratio. The ratio grows as a process waits, so long jobs are not starved.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

The scheduler is an operating system module that selects the next jobs to be admitted into the system and the next process to run. The process scheduler is a part of the operating system that decides which process runs at a certain point in time. If the scheduler cannot pause a running process and start a new process, the scheduler is a cooperative scheduler. We distinguish between long-term scheduling, medium-term scheduling, and short-term scheduling based on how often decisions must be made.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between waiting time and response time? [Round Robin])
Waiting time is the total time a process spends in the ready queue over its whole life, including every time it was preempted and had to wait again. Response time is only the time from arrival until the first time the process gets the CPU. In non-preemptive algorithms the two are equal, because the process runs to completion once started. In preemptive algorithms such as Round Robin the waiting time is usually larger than the response time.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between turnaround time and waiting time? [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion, so it includes waiting in the ready queue and actually running on the CPU. Waiting time counts only the time spent in the ready queue. Therefore turnaround time = waiting time + burst time, and turnaround time is always at least as large as waiting time.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.

SJF and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the degree of multiprogramming? [Comparison])
The degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes held in memory at once, ready to compete for the CPU. The long-term scheduler controls it by deciding how many new jobs are admitted. Too low a degree leaves the CPU idle between bursts because there are not enough ready processes to switch to; too high a degree can exhaust memory or make each process wait too long for its turn. CPU scheduling algorithms such as FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin operate on whichever processes the long-term scheduler has already admitted.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between the long-term, medium-term and short-term scheduler? [Comparison])
The long-term (job) scheduler decides which jobs are admitted into memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming. The short-term (CPU) scheduler decides which ready process runs on the CPU next and runs very frequently, so it must be fast. The medium-term scheduler swaps processes out of memory and back in to reduce the degree of multiprogramming. The algorithms FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are all short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the types of schedulers? [Comparison])
There are three types of schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler, which admits jobs into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming; the medium-term scheduler, which swaps processes out of and back into memory; and the short-term (CPU) scheduler, which chooses the next ready process to run and runs very often. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. [2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[3] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) [SJF])
burst counts. Preemptive SJF is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). When a new process arrives with a next CPU burst shorter than what is left of the currently executing process, SRTF preempts the running process. Non-preemptive SJF lets the running process finish its burst. P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with burst 4, P3 at 2 with burst 9, P4 at 3 with burst 5. P1 starts at 0. At time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted. Starvation under SJF. A long process can wait indefinitely if short processes keep arriving, because there is always a shorter job to pick; this is starvation (indefinite blocking). [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does Round Robin work step by step? [Round Robin])
Put the processes in the ready queue in order of arrival. Take the process at the head. Run it for the time quantum or until it finishes, whichever is smaller. If processes arrived during that slice, add them to the queue first. If the running process still has work left, add it to the tail of the queue behind them; otherwise record its completion time. Repeat until the queue is empty.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does SRTF work step by step? [SJF])
At every instant a process arrives or finishes, look at all the ready processes including the running one, and choose the one with the smallest remaining burst time. If it is a different process from the one running, preempt the running one. Draw the Gantt chart in pieces, recording each switch. Completion times come from the last piece of each process; then waiting = completion − arrival − burst.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithms can cause starvation? [SJF])
SJF, SRTF and Priority scheduling can cause starvation: SJF and SRTF starve long jobs, and Priority scheduling starves low-priority processes. FCFS and Round Robin cannot, since every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. Aging fixes starvation in the first group.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does SJF cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. If shorter jobs keep arriving, a long job may be passed over again and again and never get the CPU. That is starvation, also called indefinite blocking. Aging, which gradually raises the priority of a waiting process, is the standard remedy.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the effect of Round Robin on average waiting time? [Round Robin])

The long-term (job) scheduler decides which jobs are admitted into memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming. The short-term (CPU) scheduler decides which ready process runs on the CPU next and runs very frequently, so it must be fast. The medium-term scheduler swaps processes out of memory and back in to reduce the degree of multiprogramming. The algorithms FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are all short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the types of schedulers? [Comparison])
There are three types of schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler, which admits jobs into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming; the medium-term scheduler, which swaps processes out of and back into memory; and the short-term (CPU) scheduler, which chooses the next ready process to run and runs very often. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SRTF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF, preemptive SJF) always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. It is preemptive: a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time takes the CPU at once. On starvation, it can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does Round Robin work step by step? [Round Robin])
Put the processes in the ready queue in order of arrival. Take the process at the head. Run it for the time quantum or until it finishes, whichever is smaller. If processes arrived during that slice, add them to the queue first. If the running process still has work left, add it to the tail of the queue behind them; otherwise record its completion time. Repeat until the queue is empty.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does SRTF work step by step? [SJF])
At every instant a process arrives or finishes, look at all the ready processes including the running one, and choose the one with the smallest remaining burst time. If it is a different process from the one running, preempt the running one. Draw the Gantt chart in pieces, recording each switch. Completion times come from the last piece of each process; then waiting = completion − arrival − burst.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.
